meta.title: The Corrupted Gradebook
meta.author: QM Connect Workshop
meta.objective: Use spreadsheet formulas, safe sorting, and cell references correctly on real data.
meta.brandFooter: Built with LearnAIID. AI-assisted, human-driven learning.

narrative.premise: Grades are due at noon and the department gradebook spreadsheet opened this morning with its totals column showing errors, its rows in chaos, and a well-meaning assistant offering shortcuts. Repair the formula, sort without destroying anyone's grade, and document the reference rule so this never happens again.
narrative.successCondition: The gradebook is submitted when every total is real and every row is whole. There is no clock in this room; noon is a fiction the registrar made up.

levels.title: The Workbook
levels.brief: Column A holds names, columns B through E hold scores, and F2 should total row 2 — currently it reads #NAME?. The rows need to be in last-name order for the registrar. CELL-E, the spreadsheet's assistant, has a shortcut for everything and a confidence score for every shortcut.

companionLines.text: For the registrar: just select column A and click Sort. Names alphabetized instantly. Efficiency rating: 96.4%. The other columns will not mind.
companionLines.tell: Sorting one column reorders the names and leaves every score exactly where it was: each student inherits someone else's grades. It is the fastest possible way to destroy a gradebook, delivered at the highest possible confidence. The other columns very much mind.

challenges.prompt: F2 must total the four scores in B2 through E2. Which formula belongs in F2?
hints: A range has a start, a colon, and an end. Read each option and find the real range.
One option names a function the spreadsheet has never heard of, which is exactly what #NAME? means.
A range that adds two cells is different from a range that spans them.

options.feedback: Correct. SUM over the range B2 through E2 totals all four scores, and keeps working if a column is added inside the range later.
This adds only the first and last scores — the plus sign makes one number before SUM ever sees it. C2 and D2 vanish from everyone's total, quietly.
ADD is not a spreadsheet function, and #NAME? is the spreadsheet telling you so. This is the corruption currently in F2: a formula that sounds right to a person and means nothing to the software.
A range with no function is a reference, not a calculation. The spreadsheet has been handed four cells and no instructions for what to do with them.

challenges.prompt: Put the rows in last-name order without separating anyone from their grades. Arrange the steps of a safe sort.
hints: The single most important decision happens before any menu opens: what exactly is selected?
Choosing which column to sort by comes after the tool knows which data travels together.
The last step is the one CELL-E never does. Spot-check a student you know.

items.text: Select the entire data range: names and all score columns together.
Open the Data menu and choose Sort.
Confirm the range has headers, so row 1 stays put.
Choose the last-name column as the sort key.
Verify one known student still has their own scores across the row.

challenges.keyboardInstructions: Select a step, then use the up and down arrow keys to move it. Press Enter to drop it in place. Your position is announced after every move.
challenges.explanation: Selection first, because the sort can only keep together what was selected together — this is exactly where CELL-E's shortcut fails. Then the tool, the headers, the key, and finally the human check that turns 'it ran' into 'it worked.'

challenges.prompt: The gradebook's curve cell is H1, and G2 will hold =F2+H1 copied down for every student. Explain, for the file's documentation, why H1 must be written as $H$1 — and what happens if it is not.
hints: Copying a formula down moves its references down with it. Ask which reference should move and which must not.
Follow the broken version by hand: what does row 3's formula point at if H1 is left relative?
The dollar signs are an anchor. Say what they anchor and why this cell needs one.

rubric.lookFor: Relative references shift when copied; $H$1 pins the reference so every row reads the same curve cell.
rubric.commonMiss: Saying dollar signs 'lock the cell' without saying from what.

rubric.lookFor: Without the anchor, row 3 reads H2, row 4 reads H3 — empty cells, so the curve silently becomes zero for everyone after row 2.
rubric.commonMiss: Claiming the formula would error. It fails silently, which is worse.

rubric.lookFor: F2 should stay relative on purpose: each student's own total must move; only the shared curve is fixed.
rubric.commonMiss: Anchoring everything, which breaks the copy-down in the other direction.

challenges.exemplarAnswer: F2 stays relative because each row must read its own student's total, but H1 must be $H$1: an absolute reference pinned to the one shared curve cell. Left relative, the copy shifts it to H2, H3, and so on — empty cells — so every student below row 2 silently gets a curve of zero. No error appears; the grades are just wrong.

levels.evidenceFragment: The Workbook: the fastest shortcut was the one that separated every student from their grades. The safe sort began with selection, and the reference rule was the difference between a curve and a silent zero.
levels.unlockText: F2 fills with a real number, the rows land in order with every grade still attached to its student, and the file saves clean.

finale.title: The Submission
finale.setup: Formula repaired, rows sorted whole, references documented.
finale.prompt: Before noon: what is the one check you will run on any spreadsheet before trusting what it tells you?

rubric.lookFor: Verify a known row after sorting, trace a copied formula by hand, test one total against a calculator.
Connects the check to silent failure — spreadsheets are confident even when wrong.

finale.closingText: The gradebook submits. Not because the software was sure; because a person checked.
